name: Project Nessie
summary: An open-source catalog for Apache Iceberg with Git-like branches, tags and commits that span every table at once, so a set of changes to many tables can be tested on a branch and then merged in one atomic step.
intro: Nessie is a Java server, built on Quarkus, that listens on port 19120. It records every change to a table, view or namespace as a commit, and each commit captures the state of all tables at that moment. A branch is a named pointer that moves with each new commit; a tag is a pointer that stays put. Creating a branch copies no data: Nessie versions the lists of files that make up each table, not the files. One commit can change many tables, and merging a branch replays all of its commits onto the target, so people reading `main` see a whole job’s changes appear at once or not at all. Conflicts are checked per table: if both branches changed the same table, a normal merge fails. Clients reach Nessie in two ways. The original Nessie API (`/api/v2`) is used by Iceberg’s `NessieCatalog`, bundled in Iceberg’s Spark and Flink runtimes since Iceberg 0.11.0, and Spark SQL extensions add commands such as `CREATE BRANCH` and `MERGE`. Since 0.90 (June 2024) Nessie also speaks the Iceberg REST protocol at `/iceberg`: the branch goes at the end of the URI (`/iceberg/dev`), and a table name can carry a branch, commit or timestamp, as in `orders@dev` or `orders#2024-07-01T00:00:00Z`. Nessie’s own guide still calls Iceberg REST support experimental.

Through Iceberg REST, Nessie writes table metadata itself and keeps the storage keys. By default it signs each S3 request for the client (S3 request signing). If you enable assume-role, it vends STS credentials scoped to the table’s location instead, which is faster and is required for Trino, which can’t use request signing. GCS and ADLS work but are marked experimental. The commit history lives in a version store: in memory by default, which loses everything on restart; PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Google Bigtable or single-node RocksDB for production; MariaDB, MySQL, CockroachDB and Cassandra as experimental options; DynamoDB in beta. Authentication (OpenID Connect bearer tokens) is off by default, and authorization rules are CEL expressions over roles, branches and table paths. Old commits keep old files alive, so cleanup has to know about every branch: a separate Nessie GC tool marks the files any live commit still uses, according to a cutoff (a number of commits, an age or a timestamp), and deletes the rest.

Dremio’s CTO Jacques Nadeau announced Nessie in October 2020 as an Apache-licensed project; it was never an Apache Software Foundation project. In 2024 Dremio said it would bring Nessie’s features into Apache Polaris and retire Nessie. That merge hasn’t happened. Dremio moved its own built-in catalog to Polaris in April 2025 and, in September 2026, wrote that its platform is built on Polaris, not Nessie, and that Nessie’s development has slowed considerably. Nessie is still maintained and not archived: 0.109.0 shipped on 8 October 2026, and versions are still 0.x.
strengths: Branches and tags over the whole catalog: change dozens of tables on a branch, check them, then publish them all at once with a merge; tags and commit IDs pin a consistent state of every table for reproducible reports and models

Multi-table transactions are built in: one commit can change many tables, and the API offers optimistic read committed, repeatable read and serializable isolation, though most engines use only the first two
Two ways in: any Iceberg REST client (PyIceberg, Trino and others) or the older Nessie catalog that ships inside Iceberg’s Spark and Flink runtimes, plus SQL branch commands in Spark and a Java CLI
A wide choice of databases for its history, from PostgreSQL to MongoDB and Bigtable, and clients never get the bucket keys: Nessie signs S3 requests or vends scoped STS credentials
limits: Uncertain future: Dremio said in October 2024 it would merge Nessie into Polaris and retire it, has since built its platform on Polaris, and wrote in September 2026 that three people wrote the human-authored commits in Nessie’s last hundred. It is not an ASF project and is still 0.x after six years
Iceberg REST support is still labeled experimental, as are GCS and ADLS; Trino needs vended credentials, and DynamoDB isn’t recommended with Iceberg REST because of its row-size limit

Merges work per table: if the same table changed on both branches, a normal merge fails (or `FORCE` overwrites it), with no row-level merging. Only Iceberg tables and views are supported; Delta Lake support was removed in 2023

Cleanup is your job: with many versions of each table live across branches, the docs say you must rely on Nessie GC, a separate tool you run regularly, with its own PostgreSQL, MariaDB or MySQL database for live sets
Defaults are for experiments: the in-memory version store loses data on restart, and authentication and authorization are both off

sections.title: Nessie and Apache Polaris
body: When Snowflake open-sourced Polaris in July 2024, Dremio said it would help bring Nessie’s capabilities into it. The Nessie team wrote in August 2024 that the intent was to contribute catalog-level versioning, Git-like semantics and multi-table transactions to Polaris. In October 2024 Dremio went further: it would merge its catalog into Polaris, “at which time Project Nessie will be retired”, as SiliconANGLE reported, quoting Dremio’s CMO: “We will treat Polaris as our catalog and we will merge Nessie into Polaris.” At that point Dremio’s commercial catalog was still based on Nessie.

What happened instead: Dremio 26.0 (April 2025) shipped a built-in catalog powered by Polaris, and Polaris became a top-level Apache project in February 2026. Dremio, which SAP finished acquiring on 6 July 2026, still lets you connect a Nessie server (0.59.0 or later) as a source. Dremio’s September 2026 catalog guide says “the modern Dremio platform is built on Apache Polaris, not Nessie”, that existing Nessie deployments keep working, and that Nessie still does catalog-level branching better than the alternatives. Nessie itself is not archived and keeps shipping releases, but it is maintained by a small group. For a new catalog, weigh branching against that maintenance outlook.

story: By 2020 data lakes were cheap and easy to start with, but lacked basics that data warehouses had. Jacques Nadeau, Dremio’s co-founder and CTO, wrote that “something as simple as atomic visibility of new files or renaming a column were surprisingly difficult”. Table formats such as Iceberg and Delta Lake had begun to fix that for one table at a time, but nothing gave consistency and transactions across tables. On 1 October 2020 Nadeau announced Project Nessie, an Apache-licensed project built on two ideas: cross-table transactions for a data lake, and a Git-like experience for tables and views. It worked with Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hive, integrated with Spark, and stored its history in DynamoDB first, because most of Dremio’s customers ran on AWS.

Iceberg bundled a Nessie catalog module into its Spark and Flink runtimes from version 0.11.0, and Dremio built Nessie into its own products, including a Nessie source in 2023. In June 2023 release 0.62.0 removed Delta Lake support, leaving Nessie Iceberg-only. 2024 brought a new Java CLI with a SQL-like syntax and MariaDB and MySQL support (0.83, May 2024), then the Iceberg REST protocol in 0.90 (June 2024), with Nessie writing table metadata itself and signing S3 requests so clients no longer needed bucket keys.

A month later Snowflake open-sourced Polaris, and Dremio said Nessie’s capabilities would move into it. In October 2024 Dremio announced it would merge Nessie into Polaris and retire it. Dremio switched its built-in catalog to Polaris in April 2025, and by September 2026 described Nessie’s development as having slowed considerably. The project kept releasing nonetheless: 0.109.0 came out on 8 October 2026.

choices.why: Teams needed to make independent changes and combine them safely. Nadeau argued that Git already provides “a reasonable and widely adopted model for exactly that”, so Nessie copied its commits, branches, tags and merges, with tables in place of files.

choices.choice: Version the catalog, not the data
choices.why: Nessie records which files belong to each table at each commit and never copies data, which works because data files are immutable. Keeping transaction management apart from table metadata is what the docs credit for scaling to millions of tables and thousands of commits per second.

choices.choice: Built for the cloud, with a pluggable store
choices.why: Nessie was designed “from day one to run at massive scale in the cloud”. DynamoDB came first because Dremio’s customers used AWS, but the commit algorithm wasn’t tied to it, so PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Bigtable, RocksDB and others followed.

choices.choice: Optimistic transactions held by the client
choices.why: The server keeps no long-lived transaction state. A client pins a commit when it starts and can record what it read; Nessie rejects the commit if any of those tables changed, which gives up to serializable isolation without server-side locks.
